pointers.sentence: All of it is in `django/utils/log.py`.
`configure_logging` is called with two settings, and what it does depends on both (`django/utils/log.py:configure_logging`).
`DEFAULT_LOGGING` configures two loggers, `"django"` and `"django.server"`, and leaves the root logger alone (`django/utils/log.py:DEFAULT_LOGGING`).
The filters read the setting each time a record passes, not when logging is configured (`django/utils/log.py:RequireDebugFalse`).
The handler's formatter, `ServerFormatter`, colours each line by the status code the server attached to the record (`django/utils/log.py:ServerFormatter.format`).

The two are applied by two separate calls, and the second is, by default, whatever the standard library makes of a second configuration over the first: a logger the project's dictionary names has its handlers replaced by the ones the dictionary gives it, and one the dictionary does not name but whose name puts it below a named one is reset, with no level, no handlers, and its records passed up (`django/utils/log.py:configure_logging`).

`response_for_exception` obtains the logger named `"django.security."` and the exception's class name as it handles a `SuspiciousOperation`, so a logger first obtained then, after the dictionary was applied, is not disabled, and here its error reaches `"mail_admins"`, the handler of the disabled `"django"`, as well as `"project"` (`django/core/handlers/exception.py:response_for_exception`).
The documentation warns of it: a disabled logger "will silently discard anything logged to it, not even propagating entries to a parent logger" (`docs/topics/logging.txt`).

A connection records queries, and logs them, when `settings.DEBUG` is true or its `force_debug_cursor` is set; otherwise its cursors are of a class that does neither (`django/db/backends/base/base.py:BaseDatabaseWrapper.queries_logged`, `django/db/backends/utils.py:CursorDebugWrapper.debug_sql`).

It calls `log_response`, which hands the message and the response's status to `log_message`, then marks the response as logged; for a response that is already marked it returns at once (`django/utils/log.py:log_response`).

When an exception of any kind but `Http404` becomes a response, the code that catches it logs the response there, with the exception attached so that the record carries a traceback (`django/core/handlers/exception.py:response_for_exception`).
Later the request handler, seeing a response with a status of 400 or more come out of the middleware chain, calls `log_response` again (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.get_response`).

When making the `ASGIRequest` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, the ASGI handler answers with a 400 before the middleware chain is reached, and logs it itself, as a warning on `"django.request"` ([The two entry points](../handlers/entry.md#an-asgi-request)) (`django/core/handlers/asgi.py:ASGIHandler.create_request`).
Before it logs, it escapes every string argument so that control characters, a line break among them, are written as escape sequences (`django/utils/log.py:log_message`).

Django 5.2.2 made `log_response` escape its positional arguments, and 5.2.3 moved the response logging that did not yet go through `log_response` onto it (`docs/releases/5.2.2.txt`, `docs/releases/5.2.3.txt`).

`AdminEmailHandler.emit` does nothing when `ADMINS` is empty, unless a subclass has replaced the method that sends, which it takes as a sign that the mail has somewhere else to go (`django/utils/log.py:AdminEmailHandler.emit`).
The message goes out through `mail_admins` (`django/utils/log.py:AdminEmailHandler.send_mail`).

`"mail_admins"` imports the class named by `DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER` when it is constructed, so that setting is read as soon as `configure_logging` applies the defaults (`django/utils/log.py:AdminEmailHandler.__init__`).

`AdminEmailHandler` takes `using=`, the alias of the mailer in `MAILERS` to send through, and `email_backend=` is deprecated: the handler refuses it beside `using=`, or once `MAILERS` is defined (`django/utils/log.py:AdminEmailHandler.__init__`).

Until 6.1 the handler always sent through a connection made to fail silently, and while `MAILERS` is not defined it still does; once it is, the handler sends through the mailer and catches only `MailerDoesNotExist`, so it no longer ignores a failure to send (`django/utils/log.py:AdminEmailHandler.send_mail`, `docs/howto/mailers-migration.txt`).
